title: Sherpa Tensing — Camp Eight: Present Perfect Continuous (B1)
description: Camp four tells you the climb is finished. Camp eight tells you how long you have been at it — and shows the mud on your boots. It is the tense for an…

hero.lede: Camp four tells you the climb is finished. Camp eight tells you how long you have been at it — and shows the mud on your boots. It is the tense for an activity that has been running right up to now, and for one that has only just stopped and left something behind that anyone can still see.

cards.head: How long, up to now
cards.body: It started in the past, it is still going, and the point is the duration.

cards.head: Just stopped — and it shows
cards.body: The activity is over, but the evidence of it is in front of you.

cards.head: The activity, not the total
cards.body: How the time was spent, rather than what came out of it.
cards.ex: "I've been reading that report." (still at it)

cards.head: Repeated, over a stretch of time
cards.body: The same thing again and again, right up to the present.

cards.head: Explaining a present state
cards.body: The cause is behind you; the result is standing in front of you.
cards.ex: "I'm exhausted. I've been packing all day."

cards.head: Temporary, and often a complaint
cards.body: With lately and recently, and when you are not pleased about it.

cards.head: Wh- questions
cards.body: How long + have / has + subject + been + -ing?

charts.head: Conjugation chart
charts.note: Three pieces, and only the first one ever changes: have or has, then been, then the -ing form. Been is fixed and the -ing is fixed, which makes this a much easier tense to build than it looks.

charts.head: For or since?
charts.note: These two words carry most of the meaning of this tense, and they are not interchangeable. For takes a length of time; since takes the moment it started.

head: Word
Takes
Examples
rows: for two hours · for a week · for ages
since dawn · since Monday · since we arrived
all morning · all day · all week

charts.head: The verbs that refuse the -ing
charts.note: State verbs describe a condition rather than an activity, and a condition cannot be in progress. When the meaning is a state, camp four takes over: have known, not have been knowing.

head: Group
Verbs
Say this instead
rows: "We have had the flat for a year."

charts.head: Three mistakes worth naming
charts.note: Almost every error with this tense is one of these three.

head: Not this
This
Why
rows: I have been living here since 2019.
English measures duration up to now with a perfect tense, never with the present continuous.
I have been knowing her for years.
I have known her for years.
State verbs refuse the continuous, so camp four takes it.
I have been reading three books.
A number is a result, and results belong to camp four.

charts.note: Camp four and camp eight both run from the past up to now. The question is only ever which half you are pointing at: the activity that filled the time, or the result sitting at the end of it.

head: Question
Present perfect continuous
Present perfect simple
rows:
The activity and how long it ran.
"I've been painting."

The finished result.
"I've painted the fence."
Often not — and it doesn't matter.
Yes. That is the point of saying it.
Never. "I've been writing three emails" is wrong.
Never — know, be, own refuse it.

charts.example: The pair that shows the whole difference: "I've been painting the fence" — there is paint in my hair and the job may not be done. "I've painted the fence" — go and look at it, it's finished. One is about me, the other about the fence.

signals.head: How long it has run
items: all morning / all day / all week

signals.head: The evidence in front of you

sections.example: A useful habit: if you can point at something in the room and say that is how I know, this is the tense. The evidence is doing the work that for and since do in the other half.

diagram.intro: The brown peg on the left is where it started — that is always a past simple event, since I arrived, since 2019. From there the band of time carries a trail of the same action happening over and over: faint behind, solid at the head, the way a moving thing smears in a still photograph. It arrives at NOW rather than stopping short of it, and past NOW it carries on fading, because this tense usually means the thing is still going — but never actually promises it. Above sits the other half of the tense in its own zone: the evidence, the thing you can point at in the room right now. Click either to see it in a sentence.

panels.head: The stretch — how long it has run
The evidence — what you can see now
items: Your hands are filthy — have you been digging?
The ground is wet. It's been raining.
I'm exhausted. I've been packing all day.

quiz.prompt: We _____ since dawn and my feet are ruined. (walk)
quiz.hint: How long, right up to now.
quiz.explain: Since dawn measures a stretch running up to now, and the point is the walking rather than any distance. Present perfect continuous.

quiz.prompt: Your hands are filthy. _____ you _____ in the garden? (dig)
quiz.explain: The activity has just stopped and left something you can see. That is what this tense is for.

quiz.prompt: I _____ that report, but I'm only halfway. (read)
quiz.explain: Have read would say the report is finished. The continuous keeps it open, which is what halfway means.

quiz.hint: Again and again, up to now.
quiz.explain: Repeated action across a period that reaches the present takes the present perfect continuous.
English measures a duration up to now with a perfect tense. "I am living here since 2019" is the commonest German-speaker error in this camp.
Know is a state verb and refuses the continuous, so the present perfect simple takes the duration instead.

quiz.hint: There is a number in the sentence.
quiz.explain: A number is a result, and results belong to the simple. Have been writing would be right without the three.

quiz.prompt: It _____ , so the path is still wet. (rain)
quiz.hint: Just stopped, evidence in front of you.
quiz.explain: The rain has stopped but its result is visible now. That present evidence is the signature of this tense.

quiz.prompt: How long _____ you _____ for the bus? (wait)
quiz.hint: The question this tense was made for.
quiz.explain: How long + present perfect continuous is the standard way to ask about a duration that reaches the present.

quiz.prompt: He _____ the gate open all week, and the sheep got out. (leave)
quiz.hint: A repeated habit, and a complaint.
quiz.explain: Repeated over a period up to now, with irritation attached. Has left would name one occasion.
Have meaning possess is a state verb, so it takes the simple: we have had it since March.
The exhaustion now is the result of the activity, which is exactly the job of the present perfect continuous.

quiz.prompt: She _____ the fence, so there's paint everywhere. (paint)
quiz.hint: About her, not about the fence.
quiz.explain: Has painted would report a finished fence. The mess points at the activity, so the continuous is right.

quiz.hint: Lately points at a recent stretch.
quiz.explain: Lately marks a period running up to now, and the negative keeps the same three pieces: haven't + been + -ing.

results: Clean run. You can hear the difference between the activity and the result, and you know which verbs refuse the -ing.
Solid progress. Worth a look back at camp four before camp ten.
Good first attempt. The continuous/simple fork is the part to read again.
